title: The Bank of Mom and Dad: Why More Parents Are Supporting Adult Children in a Tough Economy
summary: Mabel Lago and her husband are retired and in their 70s. But before they moved from New Jersey to South Carolina, they checked with their younger son—because at 39, he was still living with them. 'We could not leave him behind, because he could not afford to live on his own,' she said. Her son works hard managing a liquor store, but low wages and no benefits, plus nearly $1,000 a month for health insurance due to his Type 1 diabetes, made independence impossible. The Lagos are far from alone. A growing share of young adults are living with parents: about 20% of 25- to 34-year-olds, nearly double the rate in 2005. One analysis found a third of all those under 35 are back home, just shy of the pandemic peak. Behind this trend is a brutal economic reality. A Pew Research Center survey found 80% of Americans agree 'it's harder for young adults today to cover basic expenses.' Housing, food, and energy costs have soared, and inflation remains stubborn. Young adults also carry more student loan debt than decades ago, and while mortgage debt is similar, the median amount adjusted for inflation is larger. Parents are stepping in. An AARP survey last year found 75% of parents across income levels help support adult children—paying for cellphones, Wi-Fi, transportation, rent, or giving cash. On average, that's $7,000 a year. The Lagos gave land to their older son, 43, so he could build a house next door with money from their own inheritance. Mabel is happy to help, but it strains their budget: they've cut back on driving and stopped eating beef. 'Did we plan for that when we had our children 40 years ago? No,' she said. 'Do we plan for that now? Yes, we have to.' Researchers warn this can jeopardize parents' own retirement. Richard Johnson of AARP notes that when lower-income families divert resources to children, 'that jeopardizes their own financial futures.' It's a new normal where the path to adulthood is longer and more expensive—and the Bank of Mom and Dad is open for business.
why_it_matters: The rise of the "Bank of Mom and Dad" reveals deep economic strains that blur the line between adolescence and adulthood, potentially widening wealth gaps and forcing families to choose between supporting children today and securing their own futures.

background_read: In past decades, many young adults achieved financial independence in their early twenties, but that timeline has reversed sharply. After the Great Recession of 2008, stagnating wages, skyrocketing housing costs, and swelling student loan debt left millions unable to afford rent, let alone a home. The Pew Research Center, a nonpartisan think tank that tracks social trends, has documented how these pressures reshape American families. Type 1 diabetes, which Mabel's son has, is an autoimmune disorder requiring constant insulin management, making health insurance not just expensive but life-sustaining. The AARP, formerly the American Association of Retired Persons, is a powerful advocacy group for older adults; its surveys now frequently warn that intergenerational support, while often loving, can silently erode parents' retirement savings. This pattern echoes earlier eras when multigenerational households were common out of economic necessity, but today's version often reflects strained safety nets rather than cultural preference.

perspectives.description: Parental support allows young adults to pursue education, avoid homelessness, and eventually achieve financial independence. It strengthens family bonds and can help transfer wealth to the next generation in an otherwise unforgiving economy.

For lower-income families, supporting adult children drains limited resources and jeopardizes parents' retirement security. This creates a cycle where multiple generations struggle financially, and the burden disproportionately falls on those with the least savings.

Multigenerational living was common historically, but the modern economy's demands—coupled with stagnant wages and rising costs—have revived it as a necessity rather than a choice. This shift mirrors broader failures in labor and housing markets rather than individual shortcomings.

Policymakers might address root causes by expanding affordable housing, healthcare subsidies, and education cost reforms to reduce the burden on families. Without intervention, the trend could deepen economic inequality and delay retirement for many older Americans, straining social services further.
